issuing_office: Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER)
subject: CGMP/Finished Pharmaceuticals/Unapproved New Drug/Misbranded/Adulterated
text:
Your firm failed to ensure that laboratory records included complete data derived from all tests necessary to ensure compliance with established specifications and standards. Your firm also failed to clean, maintain, and, as appropriate for the nature of the drug, sanitize and/or sterilize equipment and utensils at appropriate intervals to prevent malfunctions or contamination that would alter the safety, identity, strength, quality, or purity of the drug product beyond the official or other established requirements (21 CFR 211.194(a) and 21 CFR 211.67(a)).

Your firm manufactures over-the-counter (OTC) topical ophthalmic drug products using aseptic processing.

Our inspection revealed systemic data falsification. Notably, we observed critical data integrity breaches in your environmental monitoring (EM), personnel monitoring (PM), and cleaning records.

Falsified Environmental Monitoring Records

Our inspection identified critical discrepancies in your surface monitoring records. Your standard operating procedure (SOP) required post-batch surface sampling at (b)(4) locations. Your firm acknowledged repeatedly submitting unexposed plates to the laboratory and confirmed that you did not perform the actual sampling. In other instances, only partial sampling was performed.

Similarly, personnel monitoring samples were not collected for production and engineering personnel who worked in the aseptic processing room. Instead, unexposed plates were submitted to the laboratory and the associated records reflected that personnel sampling had been performed.

Further, in a separate instance, active air samples for a batch were collected at incorrect locations but falsely documented as having been collected at the required locations.

These falsification practices fundamentally undermine any confidence in your microbiology data. Notably, you lacked reliable data indicating that environmental control existed in your aseptic processing operations and to support release of batches to the U.S. market. During this period, you reported 0 colony-forming unit findings across all EM and PM sampling with the exception of a single deviation following a water leakage event. In stark contrast, following discussion of deficiencies with firm management, actual plate readings conducted during the inspection (April 10 to 14, 2026) yielded numerous EM and PM samples with microbial growth, including approximately 25 ISO 5 excursions.

Falsified Cleaning Records

Your SOP required cleaning ISO 5 surfaces (b)(4) decontamination of the room. Although cleaning records documented that these activities were completed on January 23, January 30, March 10, and March 21, 2026, our inspection found no evidence that the cleaning activities were performed. Your management confirmed that the documented cleaning activities were not performed and that the records reported false information.

The profound data integrity breaches at your firm critically undermined assurance of sterility for U.S.-distributed drug products.

In your response, you state that you suspended drug production for the U.S. market and notified your U.S. distributor of the need to halt distribution. You acknowledge that EM, PM, and cleaning records were falsified. You note several root causes, including a lack of independent oversight by quality assurance personnel and insufficient real-time supervision of cleaning execution. You state that you suspended all personnel involved and engaged an independent third-party to assess the scope of the data integrity issues. Notably, throughout your response, you reference your historical viable EM data, citing the absence of adverse trends, as a key "quality indicator data" source to support your initial product impact assessment.

Your response is inadequate. Falsified EM data cannot be used for trending analysis. Therefore, your initial product impact assessment is not supportable as it relies on EM data confirmed to be unreliable. Furthermore, you have not sufficiently acknowledged the potential scope of the systemic data integrity breaches, which extended well beyond procedural gaps or individual misconduct. Widespread falsification across many staff members, multiple record types, and over an extended period of time went unchecked, reflecting a systemic quality failure and demonstrating a general failure of senior managers in your company to exercise their responsibility to ensure integrity of manufacturing and laboratory records.

In response to this letter, provide:

A comprehensive, independent assessment of your laboratory practices, procedures, methods, equipment, documentation, supervisory oversight, and analyst competencies. Based on this review, provide a detailed plan to remediate and evaluate the effectiveness of your laboratory system.

A comprehensive, independent assessment of documentation systems used throughout your manufacturing and laboratory operations to determine where documentation practices are insufficient. Include a detailed corrective action and preventive action (CAPA) plan that comprehensively remediates your firm's documentation practices to ensure you retain contemporaneous, attributable, legible, complete, original, and accurate records throughout your operation.

A comprehensive CAPA, overseen by a qualified consultant, for handling microbiological sampling media to ensure robust and reliable data. Establish a system that ensures uncompromised and uninterrupted custody, with full reconciliation of all microbiological samples including, but not limited to, the following: o Unique labeling of each sample o Signatures of all staff who handle the sample o Complete tracking of uncompromised sample integrity and custody o Date and time of each activity (e.g., sample collection, transport, delivery, incubation, removal from incubator) o Digital time-stamped photos of all plates o Laboratory tools and methods to optimize visibility and detectability of colonies on plates o Signatures of personnel performing reading of microbial counts o Provisions for verifications and routine quality assurance oversight

An independent assessment and remediation plan for your CAPA program. Provide a report that evaluates whether the program includes effective root cause analysis, ensures CAPA effectiveness, analyzes investigations trends, improves the CAPA program whenever needed, ensures final quality unit (QU) decision authority, and is fully supported by executive management.

An independent review of your antimicrobial effectiveness testing (AET) program, including assuring that all (b)(4) products are evaluated using sound AET study protocols and that each formulation is suitable throughout its use period.

A comprehensive assessment and CAPA, overseen by a qualified consultant, for your cleaning and disinfection program. Establish a system that ensures robust cleaning and disinfection and full verification and reconciliation of all related activities, including, but not limited to, provisions for meaningful independent verifications of cleaning and disinfection execution (using appropriate methods at required locations and frequencies) and effective routine quality assurance oversight.

issuing_office: Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER)
subject: CGMP/Finished Pharmaceuticals/Unapproved New Drug/Misbranded/Adulterated
text:
Your firm failed to establish and follow appropriate written procedures that are designed to prevent microbiological contamination of drug products purporting to be sterile, and that include validation of all aseptic and sterilization processes. Your firm also failed to use equipment in the manufacture, processing, packing, or holding of drug products that is of appropriate design, adequate size, and suitably located to facilitate operations for its intended use and for its cleaning and maintenance (21 CFR 211.113(b) and 21 CFR 211.63).

Your firm failed to adequately design, control, and supervise your aseptic processing line.

Poor Aseptic Practices and Cleanroom Behavior

We observed numerous poor aseptic practices across multiple batches, operators, and dates during the manufacture of U.S.-marketed ophthalmic drug products including, but not limited to, the following:

A gowned operator stood inside the ISO 5 area near the (b)(4) , picking up exposed open sterile bottles with (b)(4) and reintroducing them into the bottle supply rather than rejecting them.

Operators repeatedly used (b)(4) directly above and in contact with open bottles and critical surfaces during undocumented interventions without rejecting the exposed containers.

Operators removed partially used open sterile (b)(4) packaging component bags from the ISO 5 area following batch manufacture, stored in the ISO 7 area for up to (b)(4) , and reintroduced to future batches without following appropriate practices to ensure the contents remained sterile.

These interventions were not documented in the batch record. Many interventions occurred in the (b)(4) area where equipment, including the (b)(4) and conveyer, directly contacted sterile open bottles. Despite the frequency of (b)(4) interventions in this area, you only performed infrequent decontamination (e.g., (b)(4) ) of the sterile (b)(4) area of the aseptic processing line.

In addition, we observed multiple deficiencies in aseptic processing operator gowning.

These and other inspectional findings indicated a lack of adequate supervisory oversight of your aseptic processing operations.

Inadequate Equipment Design

We also noted equipment design deficiencies and a lack of unidirectional airflow. For example, the position of the (b)(4) obstructed unidirectional airflow to the sterile (b)(4) in the (b)(4) , leading to inadequate ISO 5 protection of sterile (b)(4) packaging components.

Your aseptic manufacturing processes should be designed, and operations executed, to prevent contamination hazards to your sterile product. Flaws in the design of cleanrooms and aseptic processing lines, or improper execution of aseptic operations, can promote influx of contamination into the critical processing area.

These significant deviations in aseptic processes and disinfection are a further indication of insufficient control of aseptic processing operations to assure drug product sterility.

In your response, you state that operator practices did not consistently align with your procedures, and that you will be remediating your qualification program for both operators and direct supervisors. You also acknowledge deficiencies in your smoke studies. To help address these deficiencies, you commit to engaging independent third-party experts to assess your operation, including aseptic practices. You also commit to conducting all future smoke studies using a qualified, neutrally buoyant smoke agent and to implementing corrective actions, including potential design modifications, based on the outcome of airflow evaluation. Your response also commits to working with the vendor to ensure the entire ISO 5 (grade A) zone for the sterile product can be decontaminated (b)(4) .

Your response is inadequate because it does not adequately address the scope and root cause of the poor aseptic practices observed.

See FDA's guidance document Sterile Drug Products Produced by Aseptic Processing-Current Good Manufacturing Practice to help you meet the CGMP requirements when manufacturing sterile drugs using aseptic processing at https://www.fda.gov/media/71026/download.

In response to this letter, provide:

A comprehensive, independent risk assessment of all contamination hazards with respect to your aseptic processes, equipment, and facilities, including but not limited to, the following: o All human interactions within the ISO 5 area (e.g., risk reduction or elimination of (b)(4) interventions wherever possible) o Equipment suitability (e.g., reliability, capability, ergonomics, placement) and sufficient cleanroom space o Air quality in the ISO 5 area and surrounding room including, but not limited to, air volume and flow o Facility layout o Personnel flow and material flow (movement throughout all rooms used to conduct and support sterile operations, and all material transfers) o Disinfection practices and procedures o Specific CAPA recommendations that will comprehensively address the design and control hazards identified in the risk assessment

A detailed remediation plan with timelines to address the findings of the contamination hazards risk assessment. Describe specific tangible improvements to be made to aseptic processing operation design and control at your facility and explain how CAPA plan will robustly remediate your deficient sterile manufacturing operations. Include comprehensive changes to the design of both your aseptic processing lines and cleanrooms. Also, describe your plans for qualification and validation of your extensively remediated operations.

Your systematic plan to assure adherence to appropriate aseptic practices, cleanroom behavior, and written procedures, including but not limited to an independent assessment of the following with accompanying CAPA: o Suitability of actual practices based on extensive retrospective review and prospective observation of aseptic processing operations o Deficiencies in production management oversight and identification of specific improvements to ensure effective and routine supervisory oversight for all batches o Frequency and depth of QU oversight (e.g., audit, ad hoc, daily interactions) of aseptic processing and its support operations o Adequacy of written procedures and operational ergonomics o The assessment should also evaluate how poor aseptic technique and cleanroom behavior may have affected the quality and sterility of your drugs.

Perform a critical evaluation of airflow unidirectionality in your aseptic process with the assistance of a qualified consultant. Ensure smoke studies are conducted under dynamic conditions with thorough and complete evaluations of aseptic processing line airflow unidirectionality, including the impact of dynamic interactions and aseptic interventions. These thorough smoke studies should be performed after you remediate your aseptic operation and conducted using proper practices, including neutrally buoyant media, to appropriately visualize airflow.

Your CAPA plan to implement routine, vigilant operations management oversight of facilities and equipment. This plan should ensure, among other things, prompt detection of equipment/facilities performance issues, effective execution of repairs, adherence to appropriate preventive maintenance schedules, timely technological upgrades to the equipment/facility infrastructure, enhanced production floor supervision, and improved systems for ongoing management review.

A comprehensive assessment and remediation plan to ensure your QU is given the authority and resources to effectively function, that includes, but is not limited to, the following: o A determination of whether procedures used by your firm are robust and appropriate o Provisions for QU oversight throughout your operations to ensure satisfactory procedures and adherence to appropriate practices o A complete and final review of each batch and its related information before the QU disposition decision o Oversight and approval of investigations and discharging of all other QU duties to ensure identity, strength, quality, and purity of all products o Also, describe how executive management will support robust quality assurance at your firm, including but not limited to timely provision of resources that enable proactive detection and resolution of emerging manufacturing/quality issues to assure a continuing state of control.

issuing_office: Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER)
subject: CGMP/Finished Pharmaceuticals/Unapproved New Drug/Misbranded/Adulterated
text:
Your firm failed to thoroughly investigate any unexplained discrepancy or failure of a batch or any of its components to meet any of its specifications, whether or not the batch has already been distributed (21 CFR 211.192).

Your firm failed to adequately investigate out-of-limit 100% visual inspection findings for two batches of sterile ophthalmic drug products that exceeded the (b)(4) % total reject limit. Rather than conducting a full 100% re-inspection, only (b)(4) units per batch were re-inspected, and the investigations did not characterize the nature, composition, or source of the particles. Both batches were released and shipped to the U.S. market without determining whether the particles were intrinsic, extrinsic, or inherent.

Ophthalmic products operations should be designed to prevent particle contamination and to protect consumers from the risk of instilling potentially harmful particles into the eye. In addition, when categorizing any visible particles, extrinsic or foreign matter should receive special attention, as it may indicate possible microbial contamination. Microbes introduced directly into the eye can pose a serious risk to consumers. Irreversible damage, including partial vision loss or blindness, can occur and, in some cases, may progress to life-threatening systemic infection.

In your response, you acknowledge that your investigations were inadequate and that samples sent to an external laboratory for Fourier-Transform Infrared spectroscopic analysis could not conclusively determine the composition or source of the particles. While you identified a statistical correlation between high reject rates lots and a specific (b)(4) container supplier, the particle source(s) was not confirmed through analytical testing.

Your response is inadequate. The identification of particles and their sources remained inconclusive and incomplete at the time of your initial response. Your response also did not address your decision to release batches despite your significant adverse quality defect trends.

A substantial number of consumer complaints have been received since 2019, including reports of leakage, burning and stinging sensation, worsening eye redness, blurry vision, and reports of foreign matter or "floating matter." Your firm recorded "no need" or "NA" for corrective action for those customer complaints.

In response to this letter, provide:

A comprehensive, independent assessment of your overall system for investigating deviations, discrepancies, complaints, out-of-specification results, out-of-limit results, and failures. Provide a detailed action plan to remediate this system. Your action plan should include, but not be limited to, significant improvements in investigation competencies, scope determination, root cause evaluation, CAPA effectiveness, QU oversight, and written procedures. Address how your firm will ensure all phases of investigations are appropriately conducted.

A comprehensive, independent assessment and remediation plan for your visual inspection program to ensure compliance with CGMP. The assessment and remediation should include, but not be limited to, the following: o Implementing enhancements to your 100% visible inspection program, including defining critical, major, and minor defects and the individual defect limits for drug products. o Ensuring adequate methods, equipment, and personnel qualifications to reproducibly detect visible particulates, including particulates historically found in your operation. o Conducting rigorous qualification studies to ensure your (b)(4) visible particulate inspection systems consistently and reproducibly detect the variety of visible particulates encountered in your drug products. o Implementing destructive testing and other advanced technologies (e.g., (b)(4) ) as appropriate, with statistically significant sample sizes, for drug products that are difficult to inspect (e.g., (b)(4) containers). o Incorporating product-specific knowledge, process experience, deviation investigation analysis, recall/complaint data, and quality risk management to improve the visual inspection program. o Remediating your visual inspection program, including establishing new written procedures, equipment, and methods. Include a summary of the review and recommendations made by your independent consultant.

The following are violations identified during our review. As a reminder, this is not an all-inclusive list of violations that may exist in connection with your products or operations.

subject: CGMP/QSR/Medical Devices/Adulterated
text:
Failure to establish and maintain procedures for validating the device design to ensure that devices conform to defined user needs and intended uses and validation shall include testing of production units under actual or simulated use conditions, as required by 21 CFR 820.30(g). For example, a. At the Shirakawa facility, your firm failed to identify and control known catastrophic hazards in your risk management documentation and failed to validate the device design under actual or simulated use conditions for the UHI-4 insufflator. Catastrophic hazards, including air embolism, arrhythmia, and patient death, were identified through Health Hazard Assessments and complaint investigations associated with CAPA-201353; however, your Risk Management Report (DC00067142, dated November 6, 2025) did not reflect these hazards or ensure implementation of appropriate risk control measures, even after a confirmed patient death and Class I recall of UHI-4 units in 2023. Further, your design validation did not simulate actual or worst-case use conditions related to pressure sensor failure or inaccurate pressure measurements to ensure that the device would operate safely. As a result, devices distributed had design deficiencies that contributed to overpressure events during clinical use.

The adequacy of your firm's response cannot be determined. Your response states that design-related deficiencies are being addressed through global CAPAs, including CAPA-204150 (design control) and CAPA-203525 (risk management), and that a traceability matrix for the UHI-4 will be developed to evaluate design requirements, verification, and validation. You also indicate that additional design verification and/or validation testing will be performed as needed and that potential design changes will be assessed by the design owner (Olympus Hachioji). However, these activities remain ongoing, and you have not provided objective evidence demonstrating that design validation deficiencies have been corrected or that revised validation activities adequately address identified risks, including overpressure conditions. Additionally, corrective actions have been deferred to global CAPAs and another facility, and no documentation has been provided demonstrating completion or effectiveness of these actions.

subject: CGMP/QSR/Medical Devices/Adulterated
text:
Failure to establish and maintain procedures for validating the device design to ensure that devices conform to defined user needs and intended uses and validation shall include testing of production units under actual or simulated use conditions, as required by 21 CFR 820.30(g). For example, b. At the Aomori facility, your firm failed to identify and assess known hazards in the risk management documentation and failed to establish risk control measures for manufacturing processes for the Sphincterotome. In your risk management report (E_V-KD_ Risk Management Report _Rev.27), the corresponding risk line ID (KD-G158-00) identifies the potential patient harm as "Delay in Treatment" for complaints of deformed wires but fails to include the higher risk identified through analysis of Medical Device Reports of unintended cutting of blood vessels leading to patient bleeding. It also fails to identify any risk control measures for the manufacture of the wire for the Sphincterotome. Additionally, the risk management report (DC00609260_20250910) does not include the known hazard of failure of the Automated Optical Inspection system to detect nonconforming Sphincterotome products (KD-V400 Series) with burrs and flakes and does not include risk control measures for this hazard, which can lead to tissue damage and procedural complications.

The adequacy of your firm's response cannot be determined at this time. Your firm has not provided an updated Risk Management Report (DC00609260_20250910) to address the hazard and implement risk control measures for failure of the Automated Optical Inspection system to detect nonconforming Sphincterotome products (KD-V400 Series) with burrs and flakes. Additionally, your firm has not provided an updated risk management report (E_V-KD_ Risk Management Report ) to address the risk of unintended cutting of blood vessels leading to patient bleeding and risk control measures for manufacture of the wire.

subject: CGMP/QSR/Medical Devices/Adulterated
text:
Failure to establish and maintain procedures for validating the device design to ensure that devices conform to defined user needs and intended uses and validation shall include testing of production units under actual or simulated use conditions, as required by 21 CFR 820.30(g). For example, c. text:
Your firm failed to ensure that laboratory records included complete data derived from all tests necessary to ensure compliance with established specifications and standards (21 CFR 211.194(a)).

Your firm conducts microbiological analyses of components and drug products for your customers.

You perform (b)(4) pour plate methods for microbial enumeration of (b)(4) samples. During the inspection, our investigator observed that your microbiologist failed to record the (b)(4) results when they were assessed as too numerous to count (TNTC), recording only the pour plate counts. The investigator also noted that while the (b)(4) for the pour plate samples was cracked and desiccated, the pour plate counts were recorded as within acceptable limits. When (b)(4) plates are desiccated and cracked, the media can no longer reliably support uniform microbial growth. A result recorded from a compromised plate, even one that falls within specification, cannot be considered valid, as the physical condition of the media may have suppressed or obscured actual microbial recovery.

A comprehensive independent assessment of your laboratory practices, procedures, methods, equipment, documentation, and analyst competencies. Based on this review, provide a detailed plan to remediate and evaluate the effectiveness of your laboratory system.

A comprehensive assessment of documentation systems used throughout your manufacturing and laboratory operations to determine where documentation practices are insufficient. Include a detailed corrective action and preventive action (CAPA) plan that comprehensively remediates your firm's documentation practices to ensure you retain attributable, legible, complete, original, accurate, contemporaneous records throughout your operation.

For example, in November 2025, you obtained OOS microbiological results for (b)(4) lots (b)(4) . You prepared (b)(4) independent samples from each lot. You tested (b)(4) of the samples for total aerobic microbial count and the (b)(4) samples for total yeast and mold count. You did not perform an appropriate investigation into the OOS results. You also revised your microbiological sampling plan to allow for averaging of test results for component testing. This practice is not in accordance with the United States Pharmacopeia <61> test method and is unacceptable as it obscures the detection of non-uniform microbiological contamination within a lot. You subsequently released (b)(4) lots and used them in the manufacture of (b)(4) Lot (b)(4) , distributed in (b)(4) .

Notably, on (b)(4) , your customer, (b)(4) , initiated a Class I recall of (b)(4) lots of (b)(4) manufactured at your facility due to potential fungal contamination in your (b)(4) . The investigation associated with this recall is inadequate. For example, you implemented (b)(4) of incoming (b)(4) prior to filling to reduce bioburden, but subsequent OOS microbiological results obtained from (b)(4) lots demonstrate this corrective action was ineffective. Additionally, your change control associated with the (b)(4) process did not include ensuring appropriate validation of the process as well as evaluation of the (b)(4) .

Further, you lacked cleaning procedures for the (b)(4) line, did not conduct cleaning validation of the (b)(4) line, and failed to include yeast and mold microbiological testing as part of your environmental monitoring program. Though your investigation into the potential fungal contamination documented an evaluation of the cleaning procedures and environmental monitoring, it did not identify nor appropriately follow-up on these risks related to potential mold contamination.

Also provide the updated environmental monitoring study (WI-00480 Environmental Monitoring (Microbial) of Manufacturing and Laboratory Facilities Rev. 24) referenced in your response indicating sample locations, frequency, and duration, as well as alert and action limits.

A comprehensive, independent assessment of the design and control of your firm's manufacturing operations with a detailed and thorough review of all microbiological hazards.

A detailed risk assessment addressing the hazards posed by distributing drug products with potentially objectionable contamination. Specify actions you will take in response to the risk assessment, such as customer notifications and product recalls.

Complete investigations into all batches with potential objectionable microbial contamination or an OOS microbiological result whether or not later invalidated. The investigations should detail your findings regarding the root causes of the contamination.

A summary of results from testing retain samples of all drug product batches within expiry. You should test microbiological quality (total counts and identification of bioburden to detect any objectionable microbes) of each batch. If testing yields an OOS result, indicate the corrective actions you will take, including notifying customers and initiating recalls.

text:
Your firm failed to establish and follow appropriate written procedures that are designed to prevent microbiological contamination of drug products purporting to be sterile, and that include validation of all aseptic and sterilization processes (21 CFR 211.113(b)).

Poor Aseptic Practices and Cleanroom Behavior

You manufacture sterile, (b)(4) drug products (including (b)(4) ). We observed poor aseptic practices during set-up and filling operations including, but not limited to:

Operators repeatedly broke first air by reaching their arms, torsos, and heads over open sterile tubes, (b)(4) , and open (b)(4) during (b)(4) interventions.

Operators used (b)(4) directly over open bottles, (b)(4) , and caps.

An operator was observed working in the Grade A area of the (b)(4) line wearing a visibly stained gown.

Inadequate Smoke Studies

Dynamic airflow visualization (smoke) studies demonstrated that airflow patterns failed to adequately protect the aseptic processing line, including exposed sterile product and product contact equipment, from significant contamination hazards.

For example, your dynamic smoke studies did not demonstrate unidirectional airflow protection of the production line when barrier (b)(4) were open. The studies showed air moving at a sharp angle upward toward return vents, leaving critical areas of your aseptic processing lines unprotected throughout the period in which the (b)(4) are opened. This fundamental design flaw enables the entrainment of lower-quality air from the surrounding lower-classified (Class 10,000/ISO 7) cleanroom into the Class 100 (ISO 5) aseptic processing line, posing a severe risk to product sterility.

We also observed other design flaws in your production equipment that led to poor ergonomics and deficient aseptic practices that compromised unidirectional airflow.

In addition, smoke studies were incomplete, as they failed to sufficiently evaluate airflow directionality during critical aseptic processing activities.

In your response, you state you will assess and redesign your (b)(4) filling line (b)(4) to address deficiencies noted by FDA, and you will perform smoke studies on the newly redesigned line. Additionally, you state you will conduct extensive classroom and hands-on training, along with qualification to improve aseptic operator behavior.

We acknowledge your commitment to redesigning the (b)(4) solution line, and your decision to decommission your (b)(4) solution lines.

Your response is inadequate. It lacks a comprehensive program to effectively monitor personnel practices during commercial production, which is especially concerning given our past inspectional findings of poor aseptic behavior.

Further, your response failed to provide sufficient plans to improve your airflow visualization program. Notably, your response lacked adequate provisions to improve quality assurance oversight, and ensure thorough and objective evaluation of future airflow unidirectionality studies by qualified subject matter experts.

Your aseptic manufacturing processes should be designed, and operations executed, to prevent contamination hazards to your sterile product. Flaws in the design of cleanrooms and aseptic processing lines, or improper execution of aseptic operations can promote influx of contamination into the critical processing area.

In response to this letter, provide:

Your systematic plan to assure adherence to appropriate aseptic practices, cleanroom behavior, and written procedures, including but not limited to an independent assessment of the following with accompanying corrective action and preventive action (CAPA): o Suitability of actual practices based on extensive retrospective review and prospective observation of aseptic processing operations. o Deficiencies in production management oversight, and identification of specific improvements to ensure effective and routine supervisory oversight for all batches. o Frequency and depth of quality unit (QU) oversight (e.g., audit, ad hoc, daily interactions) of aseptic processing and its support operations. o Adequacy of written procedures and operational ergonomics. o The assessment should also evaluate how poor aseptic technique and cleanroom behavior may have affected the quality and sterility of your drugs.

An independent, comprehensive evaluation of airflow unidirectionality in your aseptic processing operations. Ensure smoke studies are conducted under dynamic conditions with thorough and complete evaluations of aseptic processing line airflow unidirectionality, including the impact of aseptic interventions and dynamic interactions with the surrounding cleanroom. Conduct these smoke studies after you remediate your aseptic operation and using proper practices (e.g., neutrally buoyant media) to appropriately visualize airflow.

subject: CGMP/Finished Pharmaceuticals/Adulterated
text:
Your firm failed to have separate or defined areas or such other control systems necessary to prevent contamination or mix-ups (21 CFR 211.42(c)), and your firm failed to establish and follow adequate control procedures to monitor the output and to validate the performance of those manufacturing processes that may be responsible for causing variability in the characteristics of in-process material and the drug product (21 CFR 211.110(a)).

Inadequate Equipment Cleaning and Sterilization

Your aseptic processing operation is inadequately designed to prevent contamination of your sterile (b)(4) drug products.

For example, you did not appropriately sterilize critical container-closure contact surfaces, such as the (b)(4) , bowl, track and (b)(4) equipment, as well as the (b)(4) , bowl, track, and (b)(4) equipment. Instead, you wipe these surfaces with sporicidal disinfectants.

To ensure sterility, it is imperative that only sterilized equipment comes into direct contact with the sterile formulation, containers, and closures.

Inadequate Environmental Monitoring

You also failed to ensure adequate environmental monitoring (EM) of classified areas used for aseptic production of sterile (b)(4) drug products.

The EM program used to monitor critical areas was deficient. You failed to demonstrate that the locations and frequencies established for viable air sampling, surface monitoring, and non-viable particulate sampling were adequately justified and sufficient to promptly detect contamination risks. For example, sampling was not adequate to evaluate the environment in proximity to containers and closures, nor on the surfaces of barriers facing your ISO 5 (Grade A) spaces.

Because you had not established a sufficient EM program, you lacked evidence of daily environmental control that is foundational to assuring sterility of aseptically processed products.

A vigilant, ongoing personnel and environmental monitoring program is essential to detect and respond to potential product contamination hazards in your manufacturing environment in a timely manner. Loss of environmental control in an aseptic manufacturing facility can ultimately pose a serious hazard to patients.

Inadequate Visual Inspection Program

Your visual inspection program for sterile (b)(4) drug products was deficient. Your firm failed to routinely categorize defects as part of your visual inspection program. In addition, you did not establish appropriate acceptance criteria. Notably, your process has experienced significant defect rates.

It is important that visible particulate contamination is appropriately evaluated. When categorizing visible particles, extrinsic or foreign matter should receive special attention, as it may indicate possible insanitary or microbial contamination. Sterile manufacturing operations should be designed to prevent foreign contaminants, and such contamination should trigger a thorough investigation and appropriate CAPA.

In your response, you state you will assess your (b)(4) filling line and improve its design. You state you will also revise cleaning and disinfection procedures, and conduct an EM risk assessment and subsequent EM performance qualification. Additionally, your response commits to improvements in visual inspection equipment, with better categorization of rejects and established acceptance criteria.

Your response is inadequate. It fails to systematically address the need for robust aseptic processing operations and collection of more meaningful data to support aseptic operational control. It also lacks details describing how you will ensure use of sterilizable equipment in the future and conduct EM with sufficient frequency at locations where significant activity or exposure occurs during aseptic production. Additionally, you failed to provide the details of your improved visual inspection program, including how you will ensure thorough investigations, when appropriate.

In response to this letter, provide:

A comprehensive, independent risk assessment of all contamination hazards with respect to your aseptic processes, equipment, and facilities, including but not limited to: o All human interactions within the ISO 5 area (e.g., risk reduction or elimination of (b)(4) interventions wherever possible) o Equipment suitability (e.g., reliability, capability, ergonomics, placement) and sufficient cleanroom space o Air quality in the ISO 5 area and surrounding room including, but not limited to, air volume and flow o Facility layout o Personnel Flow and Material Flow (movement throughout all rooms used to conduct and support sterile operations, and all material transfers) o Disinfection practices and procedures o Specific CAPA recommendations that will comprehensively address the design and control hazards identified in the risk assessment

A detailed remediation plan with timelines to address the findings of the contamination hazards risk assessment. Describe specific tangible improvements to be made to aseptic processing operation design and control at your facility and explain how this CAPA plan will robustly remediate your deficient sterile manufacturing operations. Include comprehensive changes to the design of (b)(4) your aseptic processing lines and cleanrooms. Also, describe your plans for qualification and validation of your extensively remediated operations.

A CAPA plan, based on the retrospective assessment of your cleaning and disinfection program, that includes appropriate remediations to your cleaning and disinfection processes and practices, and timelines for completion. Include the following as part of the assessment and CAPA plan: o A detailed summary of vulnerabilities in your process for lifecycle management of equipment cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization o A list of improvements, with an explanation how each will enhance cleaning and disinfection effectiveness o Improved ongoing verification of proper cleaning and disinfection execution o And, any other needed remediations

A comprehensive, independent assessment and remediation plan for your drug product visual inspection program to ensure compliance with CGMP. The assessment and remediation should include, but not be limited to, the following: o Implement enhancements to your 100% visible particulate inspection practices, including defining critical, major, and minor defects and establish associated individual defect limits. o Ensure adequate methods, equipment, and personnel qualifications to reproducibly detect visible particulates, include particulates which historically have been found in your operation. o Conduct rigorous qualification studies to ensure your (b)(4) visible particulate inspection systems consistently and reproducibly detect the variety of visible particulates encountered in your drug products. o For drug products that are difficult to inspect (e.g., (b)(4) containers), implement destructive testing and other advanced technologies (e.g., (b)(4) ) as appropriate, with statistically significant sample sizes to test for defects. o Incorporate product-specific knowledge, process experience, deviation investigation analysis, complaint data, recall data, and quality risk management to improve the visual inspection program. o Associated remediations to your visual inspection program, including newly established written procedures, equipment, and methods. Include a summary of the review and recommendations made by your independent consultant.

Your firm failed to perform operations within specifically defined areas of adequate size and to have separate or defined areas or such other control systems necessary to prevent contamination or mix-ups (21 CFR 211.42(c)).

You manufacture various injectable drugs products including cephalosporins (a beta-lactam drug product) and (b)(4) drug products at your facility. You failed to ensure complete and comprehensive separation of cephalosporin and (b)(4) drug products in this shared facility.

Lack of Complete and Comprehensive Separation

Your facilities and controls were inadequate to prevent the conditions that would allow for cephalosporin contamination of (b)(4) drugs.

Your building is divided into (b)(4) beta lactams, (b)(4) production. These building segments are separated by a physical wall that you consider to be fully sealed, along with dedicated HVAC units.

However, since January 2025, your environmental monitoring (EM) program used to monitor containment of beta-lactam drug products has detected cephalosporin in several instances and in multiple areas of the (b)(4) side of the building.

Inadequate Cephalosporin Monitoring

While your monitoring program detected recurring cross-contamination, it was inadequate to promptly detect loss of containment and cephalosporin contamination in your facility. For example:

EM sampling was insufficient in both number and location.

Swab sampling qualification was inadequate to assure low-level recovery.

Samples were evaluated beyond established solution stability time allowances.

These inadequacies create risk for underrepresentation of true contamination hazards throughout your facility, create potential for false negative results, and inhibit meaningful data collection upon which your quality unit (QU) can make sound risk-based decisions.

A rigorous monitoring program is essential for facility qualification, early detection of contamination hazards, and timely corrective action and preventive action (CAPA).

In addition, your testing of (b)(4) drug products for potential contamination consisted of a single unit regardless of batch size. However, contamination is generally nonuniformly distributed. Results obtained from testing a small sample size are unlikely to detect contamination that may exist in a batch exposed to the contamination hazards identified at your firm. Consequently, substantial residual uncertainty remains regarding the actual variability of contamination that may exist in batches you produce.

We also note that you mistakenly discarded multiple failing cephalosporin environmental samples before further analysis could be conducted.

In your response, you commit to strengthen investigations into positive cephalosporin findings, create a tracking form to help prevent missed samples, and improve low-level recovery. Your response also indicates that significant uncertainty remains regarding the causes of the recurring findings of facility contamination. You indicate that personnel movement was a weakness in your containment strategy while adding that personnel movement is likely not the sole contributing factor.

Your response is inadequate because it fails to adequately address how you will ensure complete and comprehensive separation. You also failed to thoroughly reevaluate your original risk management decisions, including supportive risk assessments and associated risk controls, to ensure prevention of beta-lactam cross-contamination. Although your cephalosporin and (b)(4) areas exist within the same external building structure that you claim is completely and comprehensively separated by a (b)(4) , it is essential that your design completely precludes any potential for incidental air, personnel, materials, equipment, or other interaction that could be a vector of contamination. A rigorous quality risk management program should comprehensively assess the design and determine if it provides as much protection against cross-contamination as is achieved by manufacturing in a separate building.

We note that data shared during our recall discussions revealed additional cephalosporin contamination events in the (b)(4) area, including as recently as (b)(4) .

Contamination of (b)(4) with beta-lactam drugs presents a serious risk to patient safety, including potential life-threatening (b)(4) . (b)(4) responses can occur in susceptible patients exposed to (b)(4) beta-lactams. Therefore, no safe level of beta-lactam contamination has been determined to be a tolerable risk.

Your firm failed to establish and follow appropriate written procedures that are designed to prevent microbiological contamination of drug products purporting to be sterile, and that include validation of all aseptic and sterilization processes (21 CFR 211.113(b)). Your firm also failed to perform operations within specifically defined areas of adequate size and to have separate or defined areas or such other control systems necessary to prevent contamination or mix-ups in aseptic processing areas (21 CFR 211.42(c)(10)).

You operate (b)(4) processing lines used to aseptically manufacture sterile injectable drug products for the U.S. market. Your (b)(4) were inadequately validated to ensure that they were capable of consistently (b)(4) interior surfaces of your (b)(4) lines in preparation for aseptic production. In addition, your aseptic process simulations did not sufficiently represent worst-case conditions, and you lacked adequate sampling of your ISO 5 (Grade A) area.

Biological Indicator Recoveries and Inadequate (b)(4) Validation

Inadequacies in your (b)(4) process were demonstrated through a trend of routine recoveries of biological indicator (BI) growth at the completion of (b)(4) cycle re-qualification (validation) runs since (b)(4) .

Notably, your acceptance criteria were inappropriate in that they allowed routine recovery of multiple BI survivors per re-qualification run. An adverse trend of numerous positive BIs were identified in multiple re-qualification cycles across multiple (b)(4) lines. For example, for line (b)(4) , positive BIs occurred at numerous locations ( (b)(4) of (b)(4) locations) and the positive findings included multiple replicates per location ( (b)(4) recoveries of (b)(4) replicates). In addition, other lines had similar substantial findings of positive BIs. However, you considered all re-qualification studies to be acceptable and did not further evaluate the excessive variability of your (b)(4) , including the potential impact to product. These significant recurring BI failures indicate poor (b)(4) method efficacy and require further investigation.

We also noted additional deficiencies in your (b)(4) reliability. For example:

You lacked adequate scientific justification for BI locations.

You allowed repetition of re-qualification cycles without proper investigation into observed BI growth.

You did not align with technical references you cited in your procedures.

We note that you recovered (b)(4) , from an (b)(4) inside your (b)(4) during production.

In your response, you commit to engaging a (b)(4) to help improve (b)(4) , revising acceptance criteria to align with industry standards, and initiating non-conformance reports to investigate the observed BI growth. You also commit to evaluating alternative (b)(4) technology.

Your response is inadequate in that it does not provide sufficient detail or supporting documentation to describe how adequate (b)(4) will be achieved during the interim period prior to completion of long-term remediation.

Incomplete exposure of interior surfaces to (b)(4) compromises (b)(4) effectiveness and places your (b)(4) environment at risk. The (b)(4) (Grade A) area is critical because sterile products are exposed during aseptic production and therefore vulnerable to contamination if operations are not well designed and diligently controlled. Aseptic processing operations should be designed and executed to minimize exposure of sterile articles to potential contamination hazards in the manufacturing operation. Flaws in the design or control of cleanrooms and aseptic processing operations can enable entry of contaminants into the critical (b)(4) processing area and lead to product contamination.

Inadequate Aseptic Process Simulation

The intervention of (b)(4) was simulated approximately (b)(4) times during a media fill, but production records indicate a significantly higher occurrence of this intervention.

In your response you commit to updating the minimum number of (b)(4) simulations to (b)(4) based on your 2026 retrospective review, which only covered approximately (b)(4) . Your response is inadequate as it does not ensure worst-case production activities and conditions are challenged across all (b)(4) lines. If a media fill program fails to incorporate contamination risk factors and closely simulate actual drug production, the state of process control and assurance of sterility cannot be accurately assessed.

Inadequate Environmental Monitoring

Your (b)(4) processing lines include critical operational steps conducted in (b)(4) . However, there was only a (b)(4) in one of these (b)(4) . In addition, surfaces were not monitored for microbiological contamination.

Vigilant and responsive environmental monitoring programs provide meaningful information on the state of control of the aseptic processing operation and enable an early warning system that identifies emerging contamination hazards before sterility is compromised.

Inadequate Airflow

Although your (b)(4) configurations can vary (e.g., (b)(4) bag capacity, (b)(4) configuration), you lacked airflow visualization studies in (b)(4) of your (b)(4) lines. In addition, your airflow visualization studies were insufficient (e.g., worst-case (b)(4) conditions).

We note that you have had a history of sporadic sterility test positives since 2013 (testing is routinely performed in a (b)(4) ) and persistent particulate contamination issues.

Your airflow visualization studies also revealed substantial turbulence in your (b)(4) , in which critical process steps are performed. Your firm acknowledged turbulent non-unidirectional airflow within your (b)(4) , which houses processing equipment.

Our overall findings indicate significant deficiencies in the design of your aseptic processing operation. Your current equipment, process, and airflow design pose excessive contamination risk.

Turbulent airflow may be appropriate for a (b)(4) that does not house aseptic processing equipment. In contrast, your firm uses (b)(4) that include processing line equipment.

A strong quality system is essential to oversee design and construction of aseptic processing lines, cleanrooms, and supporting utilities, and to ensure ongoing proper operational control to safeguard against contamination hazards throughout the facility lifecycle.

Well-designed aseptic processing (b)(4) represent a significant technological advance over traditional operational designs. Because all technologies have failure modes, it is essential to implement a robust design and control program that enables an ongoing state of control.

See FDA's guidance document Sterile Drug Products Produced by Aseptic Processing-Current Good Manufacturing Practice to help you meet the CGMP requirements when manufacturing sterile drugs using aseptic processing at https://www.fda.gov/media/71026/download.

In your response, you commit to improving your EM program and performing airflow visualization studies on all of your lines. You also state that you will use data from these studies to identify locations for BIs and EM.

Your response is inadequate as you lack a commitment to upgrade your manufacturing infrastructure, including equipment replacement, as part of your long-term remediation plan. In addition, the timeline for implementation of additional viable air monitoring in the (b)(4) is unclear.

A detailed program for designing, validating, maintaining, controlling and monitoring each of your (b)(4) that includes vigilant monitoring to ensure an ongoing state of control.

text:
Your firm failed to establish laboratory controls that include scientifically sound and appropriate specifications, standards, sampling plans, and test procedures designed to assure that components, drug product containers, closures, in-process materials, labeling, and drug products conform to appropriate standards of identity, strength, quality, and purity (21 CFR 211.160(b)).

Your manual visual inspection program was inadequate to reliably detect defects and ensure your sterile injectable drug products were essentially free of visible particulates.

For example, operators performing (b)(4) visual inspection were not properly qualified, as evidenced by the following:

Operators were not appropriately challenged to ensure they were capable of reliably detecting particulates within the lower end of the visible spectrum.

Particulates in challenge kits were excessively large (e.g., greater than (b)(4) microns), approximately (b)(4) times larger than what operators should be capable of reliably detecting.

Operators' rate of inspection was excessively fast (e.g., (b)(4) per unit) and did not align with the standards referenced in your procedures.

Notably, you also demonstrated poor detection rates when you used significantly longer inspection times during Acceptable Quality Limit (AQL) sampling.

Your approach to identifying product defects compromises reliable detection and the quality of data inputs to support batch release and CAPA decisions made by your quality unit.

In addition, the significant particulate matter complaints received between 2023 to 2025 indicate an inadequate visual inspection program. For example, on May 9, 2025, after testing a returned cefazolin complainant sample you confirmed foreign particulate contamination was consistent with cardboard (approximately (b)(4) mm). Your investigation concluded that inadequacies of visual inspection were a contributing cause, but you did not implement sufficient CAPA to ensure remediation of your visual inspection program.

Your investigation specifically cited potential for compromised product quality and potential patient safety risks, but stated that field action was not warranted. We acknowledge that on July 17, 2026, you agreed to voluntarily recall cefazolin, Lot LD175708, only after the Agency contacted you.

In your response you commit to enhancing your visual inspection program including performing probability of detection (PoD) studies using the (b)(4) per unit inspection duration.

Your response is inadequate. You indicate that data from post-market complaint evaluations and retain sample reviews confirm that your controls remain effective. However, you have identified particulate matter in retain and complaint samples after product was released. In addition, your response does not adequately address the spike in particulate matter defects from 2024 ( (b)(4) defects) to 2025 ( (b)(4) defects). There remains a lack of assurance that your injectable drug products are essentially free from visible particulates while you work on long-term remediation.

Visual detection of particulates is a probabilistic process that depends on, among other things, ensuring that visible particulates can be reproducibly detected by trained personnel with appropriate visual acuity. At a minimum, personnel should reliably be capable of detecting particulates of (b)(4) microns or greater at a (b)(4) % probability of detection. It is important that any visible particulate contamination is appropriately evaluated and investigated. Particulates in injectable products should be avoided through appropriate preventive measures built into your design and production controls. When categorizing any visible particles, extrinsic or foreign matter should receive special attention, as it may indicate possible microbial contamination. Extrinsic or foreign particulate contamination should occur very infrequently and trigger a thorough investigation and appropriate CAPA.

In response to this letter, provide:

A comprehensive, independent assessment and remediation plan of your systems for the visual inspection of sterile injectable drugs for defects, including the presence of particulate matter. The assessment should include acceptance and rejection criteria, personnel training, supervision, equipment and personnel qualification, equipment maintenance, and process validation, and the procedures governing them. Also include product-specific knowledge, process experience (e.g., thorough assessment of the spike of (b)(4) particulate matter defects in 2025), deviation investigation analysis, and recall/complaint data. Provide your detailed remediation action plan that includes dates by which each remediation activity will be completed and a periodic independent reassessment of the plan's effectiveness. Include a summary of the review and recommendations made by your independent consultant.

A comprehensive, independent assessment of each lot of sterile injectable drugs distributed from your facility that remains within expiry to meet the requirement of being essentially free of visible particles. This comprehensive review should include a review of all relevant in-process and finished product data obtained by your firm including all batch records.

An interim plan for risk mitigation while you perform broader studies to improve your visual inspection program. Provide a detailed list of your risk mitigations (e.g., sampling plans and methods for your proposed destructive testing).

text:
Your firm failed to thoroughly investigate any unexplained discrepancy or failure of a batch or any of its components to meet any of its specifications, whether or not the batch has already been distributed (21 CFR 211.192).

There was a pattern of inadequate investigations into critical issues, including leaking drug products and sterility failures.

Leaking Units

Your investigations into the "systemic nature" of container-closure integrity failures lacked effective CAPA to address the significantly increased rate of leak defects in your injectable drug products. You did not implement sufficient CAPA to ensure remediation of your final inspection program. Further, since 2023, media fill units were found leaking during incubation and you have received numerous leak complaints for marketed products.

All sterile drugs must be packaged using container-closure systems with robust protection that prevents the ingress of microorganisms. A product's ability to maintain integrity throughout anticipated stresses and external factors during manufacture, storage, distribution, and consumer use is critical to ensure product quality and safety. Loss of container-closure integrity is a direct cause of non-sterility.

In your response, you acknowledge that strengthening your investigation system is warranted and you will evaluate whether (b)(4) container closure integrity testing (CCIT) could be an effective layered control. You also commit to a retrospective review of critical non-conformance reports (NCR) and laboratory investigations for the last year.

Your response is inadequate. Limiting a retrospective review to (b)(4) lacks adequate scientific justification as your leak trending data illustrated the leak rate has consistently increased annually from 2023 to 2026. You also do not sufficiently address how a lack of highly capable leak detection systems impacts already produced products, or sufficiently detail improvements to your CAPA system. In addition, data from your firm indicates that although leak rate has increased, the number of NCRs opened has decreased.

Sterility Failure

Your investigation into a 2025 sterility failure for cefazolin, lot (b)(4) , assigned the root cause as a non-integral test container. Test records had been signed and dated indicating that container integrity was initially verified. However, after observing turbidity, you subsequently stated in your investigation that container integrity was not verified, classifying it as a "no-test." Without conducting a Phase II investigation, you concluded there was no risk to the manufacturing process or finished product. You invalidated the sterility result without adequate scientific justification and released this lot in July 2025.

Notably, the same container integrity problem had been observed in the sterility test of (b)(4) , lot (b)(4) , in (b)(4) , which you rejected.

In addition, a "no-test" designation was used for an (b)(4) cycle requalification attempt that resulted in numerous positive BIs.

In your response, you state your belief that the laboratory error of incubating non-integral sterility test containers was the definitive root cause. Your response is inadequate as it fails to address why your lab records described the test container as integral. It also fails to thoroughly address the lack of contemporaneous documentation of any subsequent deviation that could have theoretically occurred. You also commit to implementing a closed membrane sterility testing system in the future, but your proposal does not ensure timely remediation.

Product contamination may go undetected for substantial periods if your firm employs unreliable sterility testing practices. It should also be noted that any positive sterility test result represents a serious CGMP issue that requires a comprehensive investigation into the cause and extent of the problem, and a prompt review of the qualification status of the aseptic process.

Your firm's quality systems are inadequate. For guidance on establishing and maintaining CGMP-compliant quality systems, see FDA guidance documents: Q8(R2) Pharmaceutical Development at https://www.fda.gov/media/71535/download, Q9(R1) Quality Risk Management at https://www.fda.gov/media/167721/download, and Q10 Pharmaceutical Quality System at https://www.fda.gov/media/71553/download.

In response to this letter, provide:

A comprehensive assessment and remediation plan to ensure your QU is given the authority, independence, and resources to effectively function. The assessment should also include, but not be limited to, the following: o A determination of whether procedures used by your firm are robust and appropriate o Provisions for independent QU oversight throughout your CGMP operations to ensure satisfactory procedures and adherence to appropriate practices o A complete and final review of each batch and its related information before the QU disposition decision, including all investigations o Oversight and approval of discharging of all QU duties to ensure identity, strength, quality, and purity of all products o Also, describe how executive management supports robust quality assurance at your firm, including, but not limited to, timely provision of resources that enable proactive detection and resolution of emerging manufacturing/quality issues to assure a continuing state of control

A comprehensive, independent assessment of your overall system for investigating deviations, discrepancies, complaints, out-of-specification results, out-of-limit results, and failures. Provide a detailed action plan to remediate this system, encompassing the following: o Staff competencies (including use of appropriate subject matter experts) o Written procedures o Scientific rigor and foundation o Scope determination o Root cause evaluations o CAPA effectiveness o Quality unit lead functional roles, and oversight to ensure all phases of investigations are appropriately conducted o And, based on above, detailed systemic improvements to the investigation system

An independent third-party assessment and remediation plan for your CAPA program. Provide a report that evaluates whether the program includes effective root cause analysis, ensures CAPA effectiveness, analyzes investigation trends, improves the CAPA program when needed, implements final quality unit decisions, and is fully supported by executive management.

Provide a comprehensive, independent process capability assessment of your aseptic processing lines, with special emphasis on the capability of critical operational steps, including but not limited to, all container-closure integrity failure modes, and any related CAPA to be initiated in response to the capability assessment.

Perform a holistic assessment across your facilities for similar issues noted at this site and implement appropriate CAPA across your corporate network.

CGMP Consultant

Based upon the nature of the violations we identified at your firm, you should engage a consultant qualified as set forth in 21 CFR 211.34 to evaluate your operations and to assist your firm in meeting CGMP requirements. The qualified consultant should also perform a comprehensive six-system audit 1 of your entire operation for CGMP compliance and evaluate the completion and efficacy of your corrective actions and preventive actions before you pursue resolution of your firm's compliance status with FDA.

Your use of a consultant does not relieve your firm's obligation to comply with CGMP.

text:
Your firm failed to thoroughly investigate any unexplained discrepancy or failure of a batch or any of its components to meet any of its specifications, whether or not the batch has already been distributed (21 CFR 211.192).

Your firm manufactures over-the-counter (OTC) drug products such as (b)(4) and (b)(4) , primarily distributed by your customers as promotional items. Your firm routinely failed to investigate out-of-specification (OOS) chemical and microbiological results for drug products and for (b)(4) system monitoring samples. Your firm retested failing samples or prepared and tested new samples without justification until your analysts obtained passing results. Your firm used these results to release drug product to the market without appropriate investigations into the original failing results.

Additionally, your firm failed to conduct adequate complaint investigations. Your investigations consisted largely of email correspondence and lacked proper root cause determination and implementation of corrective actions and preventive actions (CAPA). Inadequate investigations are a repeat observation identified at your firm.

In your response, you commit to a retrospective review of the OOS results and implemented an interim "full stop" for any initial OOS result. You also state you will review prior OOS results and customer complaints to determine product impact and ensure release decisions were scientifically justified. Your response is inadequate. You failed to provide plans on how you will ensure that OOS results and complaints are always appropriately handled. You also failed to provide adequate details of your remediations to ensure they are sustainable to prevent repeat violations.

Passing retest results alone cannot serve as the basis for invalidating OOS results. As a manufacturer, you have a responsibility to fully investigate aberrant chemical and microbial test results that may impact drug product quality. For more information about handling out-of-specification and failing test results and documenting your investigations, see FDA's guidance document Investigating Out-of-Specification (OOS) Test Results for Pharmaceutical Production at https://www.fda.gov/media/158416/download.

In response to this letter, provide:

A comprehensive, independent assessment of your overall system for investigating deviations, discrepancies, complaints, OOS results, and failures. Provide a detailed action plan to remediate this system. Your action plan should include, but not be limited to, significant improvements in investigation competencies, scope determination, root cause evaluation, CAPA effectiveness, quality unit oversight, and written procedures. Address how your firm will ensure all phases of investigations are appropriately conducted.

A retrospective, independent review of all invalidated OOS (including in-process and release/stability testing) results for products currently in the U.S. market and within expiry as of the date of this letter and a report summarizing the findings of the analysis, including the following for each OOS result: o Determine whether the scientific justification and evidence relating to the invalidated OOS result conclusively or inconclusively demonstrates causative laboratory error. o For investigations that conclusively establish laboratory root cause, provide rationale and ensure that all other laboratory methods vulnerable to the same or similar root cause are identified for remediation. o For all OOS results found by the retrospective review to have an inconclusive or no root cause identified in the laboratory, include a thorough review of production (e.g., batch manufacturing records, adequacy of the manufacturing steps, suitability of equipment/facilities, variability of raw materials, process capability, deviation history, complaint history, batch failure history). Provide a summary of potential manufacturing root causes for each investigation, and any manufacturing operation improvements.

An independent assessment and remediation plan for your CAPA program. Provide a report that evaluates whether the program includes effective root cause analysis, ensures CAPA effectiveness, analyzes investigations trends, improves the CAPA program whenever needed, ensures final quality unit decision authority, and is fully supported by executive management.

A comprehensive, independent review of your overall complaint system, including a retrospective review of all complaints for the last three years from the initial date of inspection with an assessment that includes, but is not limited to: o Nature of complaint, and potential associated risk o Date of first notification and subsequent contacts with complainant o Timing and sufficiency of follow-ups with the complainant to obtain photographs and the complaint sample, as well as to obtain any additional contextual information. Determination of whether relevant complaint samples were available and extent of efforts to obtain the complaint sample. If insufficient attempts were made, identify the root cause(s) for not adequately pursuing their return. o Review of long-term history for similar or same defects. o Identification of potential causes of the defect that led to the complaint, including evaluation of whether the scientific justification and evidence relating to the identified root cause(s) were adequately documented. In the event a complaint was attributed to factors outside of the firm's control(e.g., user error), assess the strength of this determination and whether it was based on conclusive or inconclusive information.

o CAPA steps taken including, but not limited to, manufacturing/quality improvements (e.g., manufacturing operation, raw materials, supplier, quality control), as well as recalls or heightened quality surveillance (additional testing/examinations, adding batch to stability program). o For all complaint investigations found by the retrospective review to be deficient due to insufficient root cause or CAPA, perform a thorough analysis of production (e.g., batch manufacturing records, adequacy of the manufacturing steps, suitability of equipment/facilities, variability of raw materials, process capability, deviation history, complaint history, OOS result history, batch failure history). o Based upon this independent review, provide a comprehensive assessment of the complaint system that identifies all deficiencies and needed improvements.

text:
Your firm failed to establish laboratory controls that include scientifically sound and appropriate specifications, standards, sampling plans, and test procedures designed to assure that components, drug product containers, closures, in-process materials, labeling, and drug products conform to appropriate standards of identity, strength, quality, and purity (21 CFR 211.160(b)).

Your test method procedures allowed multiple retesting of samples following an OOS result, often until an acceptable result is obtained. For example, your (b)(4) standard operating procedure (SOP) described repreparing OOS samples and retesting multiple times without requiring investigations. The SOP requires notifying quality control management only after (b)(4) OOS results. Your procedure also stated that if an unidentified peak is observed during chromatographic analysis, it is at the discretion of the analyst to consult the Quality Control manager to determine whether further action is needed.

Additionally, your (b)(4) Microbial Testing SOP allows retesting following an initial failure. Also, your SOP says that if the retest fails, your analysts are to use the (b)(4) , a second microbiological testing instrument. You routinely invalidated failing batch release results from the (b)(4) system and used the passing (b)(4) results to release product to the market without scientific justification. You could not provide any data to support this tiered testing approach or the validation of one method as superior to the other.

In your response, you commit to implementing an interim requirement to open an OOS investigation for all initial failing results. You also commit to revising your OOS procedure to define when repeat testing, re-injection, re-vialing, etc. are allowed, when Quality Assurance authorization is required, and to require scientific justification and documentation of all data generated. Your response is inadequate because it fails to recognize the scope of your poor analytical practices. You did not address revisions to specific analytical methods, training, or systemic remediation of your routine practice of invalidating OOS results and retesting. Inadequate laboratory controls have previously been observed at your firm, and your earlier commitments to correct them and prevent their recurrence were not effective.

These are unscientific practices and objectionable under CGMP.

Chemical and microbial release testing, an essential quality control step, is integral in preventing distribution of unsafe products. Integrity of data is fundamentally compromised when there is a failure to record or maintain complete and accurate records of test results or conditions associated with drug testing. Furthermore, the lack of reliable data compromises the Quality Unit's (QU) ability to exercise its function of ensuring compliance with applicable standards.

In response to this letter, provide:

A comprehensive independent assessment of your laboratory practices, procedures, methods, equipment, documentation, and analyst competencies. Based on this review, provide a detailed plan to remediate and evaluate the effectiveness of your laboratory system.

A list of chemical and microbial specifications, including test methods, used to analyze each batch of your drug products before a lot disposition decision.

An action plan and timelines for conducting full chemical and microbiological testing of retain samples to determine the quality of all batches of drug product distributed in the United States that are within expiry as of the date of this letter.

A summary of all results obtained from testing retain samples from each batch. If such testing reveals substandard quality drug products, take rapid corrective actions, such as notifying customers and product recalls.

A comprehensive review and remediation plan for your OOS result investigation systems. The CAPA should include but not be limited to addressing the following: o Quality unit oversight of laboratory investigations o Identification of adverse laboratory control trends o Resolution of causes of laboratory variation o Initiation of thorough investigations of potential manufacturing causes whenever a laboratory cause cannot be conclusively identified o Adequate scoping of each investigation and its CAPA o Revised OOS investigation procedures with these and other remediations o A similar review and remediation of your system for handling out-of-limit findings (i.e., data that falls outside action limits)
